content: What are the primary scientific and operational goals this system must achieve for your users, and how will you judge whether it is successful?

The main scientific goal is to let researchers combine weather observations with ecosystem models so they can run grid-based biogeochemical simulations more efficiently and with less manual effort. Operationally, it needs to hide the complexity of the distributed computing resources, manage inputs and outputs cleanly, and give users a reliable interface for submitting runs and reviewing results.
We’d judge success by whether scientists can get through a full modeling workflow without needing IT support, whether jobs run reliably on the remote resources, and whether the results are easy to visualize and reuse. If it reduces turnaround time for analyses and people trust the outputs enough to use them in their research, that would be a strong sign it’s working.

Who are the different user and support roles that will interact with this system, and what responsibilities or permissions should each role have across data management, job submission, monitoring, and results review?

The primary users are the scientific modelers, and they should be able to upload and organize input data, configure and submit modeling runs, monitor job status, and review outputs and visualizations. I’d also expect a smaller group of technical support or system administrators who can manage accounts, resource access, and the grid-side configuration, but they shouldn’t need to touch the scientists’ modeling details unless there’s a support issue.
For permissions, scientists should control their own projects and data, while admins should have broader operational access for troubleshooting, queue management, and system health. There may also be read-only collaborators or reviewers who can view selected results without being able to change inputs or launch jobs, but that would depend on how the research groups want to collaborate.

For read-only collaborators or reviewers, what exactly should determine which results they can see, and what are the rules for sharing them—for example, is access granted per project, per result set, per run, or by some explicit approval or invitation process?

My expectation is that access would be granted explicitly, not automatically just because someone is in the same organization. The safest default would be per project, with the project owner able to share either the whole project or specific runs and result sets when there’s a reason to do that. I’d also want an invitation or approval step so we can track who can see what, especially if the data are still in progress or not meant for wider distribution.
